phase_6_ui_modularization.key_technique:
ES module named imports bind the SAME identifiers, so a declaration can move into a module and be imported back under its original name. That is what made the 122-ref hoist possible without rewriting a single reference.

The second lever: the function bodies already referenced a module-level `let game`. Making `game` a *parameter* of the extracted function means every `game.x` inside keeps resolving — to the parameter — so the bodies needed no editing at all. Only an internal self-call had to thread the parameter through.

critical_findings.summary: KILLSTREAK_REFACTOR_GUIDE.md maps `activateEngulf` to the Overdrive sword, but the function body guards on `swordId !== "devourer"` and `phase.phase < 17`. Devourer is the sword with 17 phases, so Engulf is Devourer's secondary (X) ability, not Overdrive's.
critical_findings.impact: Following the guide literally would have produced a misleading file layout (src/swords/overdrive/overdrive.ability.js containing Devourer's ability) and invited a future 'fix' that changed gameplay.
critical_findings.resolution: Extraction was driven by the guards inside each body instead of the guide's table, and the guide has now been corrected in place. Changes made to KILLSTREAK_REFACTOR_GUIDE.md: (1) the ability-mapping sentence now carries an explicit correction block naming devourer.engulf.ability.js; (2) the directory tree no longer lists overdrive.ability.js and notes Devourer's two abilities; (3) the Phase 2 dispatcher snippet was replaced with the real activatePrimary/activateSecondary API, with a warning that a swordId-keyed dispatcher would silently grant Overdrive a new skill; (4) '10 hàm start*Cutscene' was corrected to 11 in both places; (5) Phase 3 gained a note that the real scope also includes getCutsceneDialogue, advance, skip and the ~348-line finishCutscene with its unguarded phase-17 fall-through.
critical_findings.related_behaviour: Because Overdrive has no ability module, its Z input falls through to Gluttony, whose `swordId !== "devourer"` guard rejects it. Overdrive therefore has no functional Z or X ability. This is pre-existing behaviour and was preserved deliberately, not fixed.

critical_findings.summary: 31 sibling JSON files (7 swords, 22 NPCs, 2 maps) sat next to the legacy .js data scripts but were never referenced by anything: no `.json`, `fetch(` or `XMLHttpRequest` reference exists anywhere in js/ or index.html. The guide nevertheless instructs copying from the sword ones, and that is exactly what produced the stale-data-drift bug.
critical_findings.impact: Dead weight that actively misleads the refactor — the sword JSONs were the documented (and actual) source of 117 drifted values.
critical_findings.resolution: Moved out of data/ into scratch/backup/dead-data-json/, preserving their relative paths, so the trap is gone but nothing is destroyed. data/ now contains only the 31 .js data scripts the game actually loads. Verified: npm run build unaffected, runtime unaffected. FINAL: that quarantine directory has since been DELETED outright on explicit instruction — verified first that no code referenced those paths (only docs and the tracker mentioned them), that data/ held zero .json files, and that the authoritative data lives in src/**/*.data.json, derived from the data/**/*.js scripts which remain. The spent scratch/diagnose_data_drift.mjs, which read the pre-move sibling paths and was already broken by the move, went to scratch/backup/obsolete/ with it.
critical_findings.note: Moved rather than deleted because git is not installed in this environment, so a hard delete would have been unrecoverable. The folder can be deleted outright once the user is satisfied.

critical_findings.summary: Each phase's splice verifier diffed the method inventory of its own backup against the live file, so it went stale the moment a later phase edited that file again. verify_splice lost its game.js assertions after Phase 3; verify_splice_cutscenes failed after Phase 4.
critical_findings.impact: A red verifier that no longer means anything — noise that trains you to ignore failures.
critical_findings.resolution: Added scratch/verify_inventory.mjs, which compares the live files against the ORIGINAL pre-Phase-2 backups and asserts the removed set equals the union of every phase's removals (40 methods in game.js, 14 in entities.js). The per-phase verifiers now only assert their own methods are absent plus their call-site rewrites, both of which stay true across phases. All 10 harnesses exit 0.

critical_findings.summary: Phase 3 had moved the ten finishCutscene completion blocks into cutscenes.data.js, where `this.unlockAchievement(...)` became `game.unlockAchievement(...)`. Phase 5 then deleted that method from Game, leaving five dangling calls (aquatic/soil/metallic/flora/hellfire *_ascended) inside the cutscene onFinish bodies.
critical_findings.impact: A runtime TypeError every time one of those five cutscenes completed. It was masked in the observable outcome because the same achievement is also granted from onSwordPhaseUp, so the badge still appeared — the error was only visible in the console.
critical_findings.why_checks_missed_it: Every existing check passed. `npm run build` does not resolve runtime method lookups; the verify_cutscenes stub supplied an unlockAchievement method, so the new path worked in the harness while production had removed it.
critical_findings.resolution: The five calls in cutscenes.data.js now route through AchievementSystem. More importantly, scratch/verify_inventory.mjs gained a static cross-module check: it enumerates the live Game methods and asserts every `game.<name>()` call anywhere under src/ resolves to a real one (28 files scanned, comments stripped first). That check fails on exactly this class of bug.
critical_findings.lesson: A stubbed harness tests equivalence, not availability. Cross-module call targets need their own static check.

critical_findings.summary: formatNumber() recurses into itself for the Googol tier (`if (threshold === 1e100 && val >= 1000) return formatNumber(val).short + ' Googol'`). With `Infinity` as input, val stays Infinity and the recursion never terminates — RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.
critical_findings.impact: Any code path that formats a non-finite number crashes the frame. Not reachable from normal play (kills/streak are finite), so it is latent rather than live.
critical_findings.found_by: scratch/verify_utils.mjs, which deliberately included ±Infinity in its input set
critical_findings.resolution: FIXED after the refactor, on explicit instruction, once behaviour preservation stopped being the priority. formatNumber now guards `if (!Number.isFinite(n))` and returns { short: s, full: s } with s = '∞' or '-∞'. Two details worth keeping: (1) only +Infinity actually recursed — -Infinity FAILS the `val >= 1000` Googol guard, so it fell through to the garbage suffix '-Infinity Googol' instead of crashing. I asserted a crash for both and the verifier corrected me. (2) NaN's output is unchanged ('NaN'), because it never matched a threshold and already reached the same literal through the toExponential path. verify_utils.mjs now excludes ±Infinity from the parity list and asserts them as an INTENTIONAL divergence with the legacy outcomes recorded, so the difference is a documented decision rather than a silently skipped input.

critical_findings.summary: When a moved function's body calls ANOTHER function in the same slice, the call site is inside the emitted module, not js/main.js. The slice tool only rewired call sites in main.js, so the argument that the callee now takes as a parameter was never supplied. Two instances: src/ui/library.js line 40 called renderLibrarySwords() from renderLibrary, and src/ui/badges.js called renderDebugBadges() from inside its own 'Grant' click handler.
critical_findings.impact: Silent TypeError at runtime. renderLibrarySwords(game) with game undefined throws on game.player.swordId, so opening the Library modal would have crashed. The badges one is worse to spot: it only fires when a user clicks 'Grant' in the debug badge grid, and then throws on game.saveData.badges.
critical_findings.why_checks_missed_it: verify_slice.mjs asserted only that each body was verbatim and that main.js's call sites passed the new argument, and the manifest had no field describing an internal rewrite. The badges instance had already shipped in slice 5 and survived a full verifier run plus a runtime pass — the runtime pass missed it because renderDebugBadges is only reachable once isDebugUnlocked is set, which that probe never did.
critical_findings.resolution: The tool now rewrites cross-calls inside the moved bodies (per body, never across the whole source, because `export function renderLibrary(game)` would otherwise match as a call). verify_slice.mjs gained a check that no argument-less inner call to a parameterised sibling survives in any module, plus an undoInternal() normalisation so the rewrite is not mistaken for a body edit. That new check immediately caught the latent badges.js instance, which was then fixed to renderDebugBadges(game).
critical_findings.lesson: 'Body verbatim' is necessary but not sufficient. A mechanical transform can be verbatim and still wrong — the transform's own edits have to be asserted, not just the parts that did not change. A runtime probe that never reaches the code path proves nothing about it.

critical_findings.summary: The call-site rewiring inserted the argument unconditionally, turning an argument-less call into `f(game, )`. Harmless to the parser but it is noise in a refactor whose whole selling point is that the output is clean.
critical_findings.impact: Cosmetic only. Four instances had accumulated in js/main.js (renderDebugBadges) plus twelve from the library slice.
critical_findings.resolution: rewireCallArgs() now does a single pass that peeks at what follows the opening parenthesis, emitting `f(game)` for an empty argument list and `f(game, ` otherwise. Single pass is load-bearing: a second pass would re-match the text the first had just written. The four pre-existing artifacts were cleaned up by hand. verify_slice.mjs accepts both forms.

critical_findings.summary: The bestiary avatar rendering in renderLibraryNpcs is guarded by `if (canvas && window.Killstreak && window.Killstreak.NPC)`. window.Killstreak.NPC does not exist — the namespace exposes Config, Data, Entities, Game, GameInstance, I18n, MapSystem, Storage, formatNumber, game, parseNumberInput. So the guard is always false and every NPC avatar canvas stays blank.
critical_findings.impact: The bestiary renders 22 correct cards with correct stats and zones, but each avatar box is empty. Since the block is dead, the gradient fill, the circular clip and the dummy-NPC draw never run.
critical_findings.evidence: Measured in the browser: reading the avatar canvas gives 0 painted pixels, while painting the same canvas manually through the identical code path gives 1434. So the canvas is fine and the block is simply never entered.
critical_findings.resolution: FIXED after the refactor, on explicit instruction, once behaviour preservation stopped being the priority. Both references now go through the namespace that actually exists: the guard checks window.Killstreak.Entities.NPC and the constructor call is new window.Killstreak.Entities.NPC(...). Verified that Entities.NPC exists and that its signature (x, y, zoneIndex, type, slotIndex) is an exact match for the existing call (22, 22, 0, npc.id, 0) BEFORE changing anything — the parameters already lined up, which is why the dropped reference was almost certainly a namespace rename rather than a mismatch. The surrounding try/catch still degrades to a flat circle if the draw ever throws. Verified live: all 22 avatars now paint, 1434 pixels each, 0 blank — 1434 being exactly the figure recorded in this finding's original evidence, so the output matches the known-good reference rather than merely being non-zero.

critical_findings.summary: scratch/analyze_cutscenes.mjs was a one-off exploration script from Phase 3. It reads the start*Cutscene function bodies out of js/game.js, which Phase 3 emptied into src/systems/cutscenes.data.js, so it had been throwing 'startAquaticUnlockCutscene not found' ever since.
critical_findings.impact: Same class as stale-phase-verifiers: a permanently red script in a directory the developer scans for signal. It does not gate the build, but it makes 'run the suite' unreliable as a habit.
critical_findings.resolution: Moved to scratch/backup/obsolete/. The full scratch suite is green again: 16 scripts, 0 failures.

critical_findings.summary: verify_hud.mjs asserted a hardcoded '33 call sites rewired in total', counting HUD call sites in js/main.js alone. Phase 6 slice 10 moved handleApplyDebugKillstreak — which called all three HUD functions — into src/ui/debugPanel.js, so the main.js count fell to 30 and the check went red.
critical_findings.impact: Third instance of the stale-phase-verifiers class: a per-phase verifier whose scope no longer matches where the code actually lives. Nothing was broken — three call sites had simply moved.
critical_findings.why_it_matters: That count is a real invariant, not bookkeeping. It is the guard against a call site being silently dropped while rewiring arguments during extraction. The tempting 'fix' — loosening it or deleting it — would have thrown away genuine protection.
critical_findings.resolution: The check now counts across main.js plus all of src/**/*.js, excluding src/ui/hud.js where the functions are defined, and still asserts exactly 33. It keeps working as call sites continue migrating out of main.js while preserving the original guarantee that none are lost. Suite is back to 16/16.
critical_findings.lesson: When a counter guards an invariant, widen its SCOPE as code moves; do not relax the COUNT. Those are very different edits and only one of them keeps the protection.

critical_findings.summary: returnFromModal was registered as a BARE listener on 10 modal close buttons (addEventListener("click", returnFromModal)). Once the function took `game` as a parameter, each click delivered the MouseEvent as that argument. The event object is truthy, so the `if (game)` guard passed and game.setPaused(false) threw TypeError: game.setPaused is not a function.
critical_findings.impact: Every one of the 10 modal close buttons threw instead of navigating — the Library, Sword Stand, Achievements, Settings and Stats modals all became un-closable. Caught by a runtime probe, not by any static check.
critical_findings.why_checks_missed_it: The tool has a `callbacks` mechanism for exactly this, but returnFromModal was declared in `callArgs` ONLY. The verifier then compared counts of `returnFromModal(` — the 2 real calls matched the 2 rewrites, and a bare reference contains no `(` at all, so it was invisible to a call-site count. `game.setPaused` exists on the Game prototype, so the cross-module method check in verify_inventory also had nothing to report: the method was fine, the VALUE was wrong.
critical_findings.resolution: returnFromModal moved into callbacks as `{ args: 'game' }`, the 10 registrations were wrapped to `() => returnFromModal(game)`, and the slice was regenerated from its backup. verify_slice.mjs gained a check that every moved function with parameters has every bare reference in main.js wrapped (imports stripped first, since an import list mentions every name bare). Re-run across all 12 slices: returnFromModal's 10 were the only instance in the whole refactor.
critical_findings.lesson: A call-site count cannot see a registration, because a registration has no call. 'Called with the wrong argument' and 'registered as a listener' are different shapes and need different checks.

critical_findings.summary: verify_slice.mjs's undoInternal() normalises away the argument a slice inserted, so the module body still compares equal to its backup. It was applied to the module side only. But main.js.modals.bak was taken AFTER slice 11, so it already contained updateSwordStandUI(game) — and this slice deliberately left that call alone. Undoing one side invented a difference that did not exist, and openScreen reported as 'not verbatim'.
critical_findings.impact: A false failure on a correct slice, which is the dangerous direction: it invites weakening a real check to make it green.
critical_findings.resolution: undoInternal() is now applied to BOTH sides. It is idempotent for calls a previous slice already rewired (nothing to undo) and still normalises the ones this slice changed, so the comparison holds either way.

critical_findings.summary: loop(game, currentTimestamp) takes the requestAnimationFrame timestamp as its SECOND parameter, but rAF hands it to the callback as its FIRST argument. The callback wrapper inserted for slice 13 was `() => loop(game)` — it forwarded `game` and dropped the timestamp, so currentTimestamp was undefined on every frame. `dt = Math.min(0.1, (undefined - lastTimestamp) / 1000)` is therefore NaN, and Game.update(NaN) propagated NaN through the player and camera.
critical_findings.impact: Total, silent corruption of the simulation: game.player.x/y and game.camera.x/y were NaN from the first frame, and the NaN persisted because lastTimestamp was reassigned to undefined each pass. Nothing threw. The HUD still looked correct because the HP/damage portions of the loop do not use dt — which is exactly why my own runtime probe PASSED while the game was broken.
critical_findings.how_it_was_caught: Not by the probe. The probe asserted HP text and bar widths, and reported all-pass with errors: []. It was caught by noticing 'X: NaN | Y: NaN' in the minimap coordinate widget in the page snapshot, then tracing that readout to js/map.js:177, which prints Math.round(game.player.x) — the player's position, not the mouse. That is the only reason this did not ship.
critical_findings.resolution: The wrapper now forwards the timestamp: `callbacks: { loop: { event: 'ts', args: 'game' } }` produces `(ts) => loop(game, ts)`. Verified at runtime: player position is 450/650 and finite, KeyD moves x to 587.22, KeyW moves y to 512.71, and the readout tracks it as 'X: 587 | Y: 513'.
critical_findings.lesson: Two of them. (1) A wrapped callback must forward EVERY argument the original received, not just the one being injected — an extra leading parameter is a silent trap. (2) Asserting on a function's OUTPUT is not enough when the output has two independent input paths: the HUD half of loop() was fine while the simulation half was NaN. Find a signal that depends on the part you changed — reading an unrelated widget in the page snapshot is what saved this.

critical_findings.summary: The first four Phase 7 conversions left ${} inside four remaining skeletons: `class="badge-status-tag ${isUnlocked ? "unlocked" : "locked"}"` in both badges.js and library.js, `class="npc-tier-pill ${tier.cls}"` in the bestiary, and `class="btn-debug-grant" ${isUnlocked ? "disabled" : ""}` in the debug grid. The last of those interpolates an ATTRIBUTE, which is the sharpest edge of innerHTML because it can escape the attribute rather than merely the text node.
critical_findings.impact: Not exploitable with shipped data, but it meant 'Phase 7 complete' would have been false: the invariant was still violated in the exact shape the phase exists to remove. A future badge or tier name reaching one of those ternaries would have been able to break out of the attribute.
critical_findings.how_it_was_caught: By writing the invariant as a machine check (verify_phase7_innerhtml.mjs) instead of trusting a hand-written completion note. Its first run failed 4 of 6 skeletons, and because I had already fixed the failure detail to name the offending expression, it printed the ternaries directly. A note in the tracker would have claimed done.
critical_findings.resolution: Converted to classList.add(...) and setAttribute('disabled','') . Verified that the DOM-API path serialises byte-identically to the template: classList.add('unlocked') on <div class="badge-status-tag"> gives exactly 'badge-status-tag unlocked'; setAttribute('disabled','') gives exactly <button ... disabled="">. Live values asserted: 8 achievement + 8 library status tags, 22 tier pills (4 novice/4 adept/4 elite/5 dread/5 apex, matching the rank thresholds), debug grid 0 disabled when all locked and 3 disabled after granting 3 badges.
critical_findings.lesson: When a phase claims to establish an invariant, encode the invariant as a check that can fail, then believe the check over your own note. Do not relax the check to make it pass — the honest fix was four more small conversions, and the strict rule is what surfaced them.

critical_findings.summary: The phase-card title carried style="color: ${p.color};". The obvious conversion, el.style.color = p.color, is NOT equivalent: the HTML parser keeps a style attribute's text verbatim ('color: #38bdf8;') while the CSSOM re-serialises it ('color: rgb(56, 189, 248);').
critical_findings.impact: The computed colour is identical, so nothing would have looked wrong, but the serialised DOM would have differed on every phase card — turning the equivalence check into an argument about which differences are allowed instead of a clean equality.
critical_findings.how_it_was_caught: By asking the browser directly before choosing, rather than assuming: parse-via-innerHTML gives 'color: #38bdf8;', .style.color gives 'color: rgb(56, 189, 248);', setAttribute gives 'color: #38bdf8;'.
critical_findings.resolution: Used setAttribute('style', 'color: ' + p.color + ';') for the one data-derived style. The other two inline styles in that template (the weak badge and the scaled row) are constants, so they are set as literal strings.
critical_findings.lesson: Two DOM paths that look interchangeable can differ in serialisation while agreeing in rendering. Check which one the *verifier* will see, not just which one the user will see.

critical_findings.summary: The Phase 7 equivalence hashes recorded mid-session were produced by a probe that included the container element itself, while the probe kept in scratch/phase7_dom_probe.js walks only its children. The two canons give different numbers for the same DOM, and the earlier figures were about to be re-used as a before/after test.
critical_findings.impact: Would have produced a false regression signal: re-measuring the phase cards under the child-walking canon gave 4c33d6dc where the tracker recorded 432aa5ee, which looks like a broken refactor and is actually a changed oracle.
critical_findings.how_it_was_caught: Noticed that the lengths differed by hundreds of characters, far more than the root element's own attributes could account for — the hash alone would have been ambiguous, but a hash plus its canonical length is much harder to fool.
critical_findings.resolution: Re-baselined under one documented canon and recorded the canon in the probe's header and in status.phase7_dom_equivalence_baseline, including an explicit warning that the older numbers are superseded and must not be cited as a match. Stored the canonical string LENGTH alongside every hash from then on.
critical_findings.lesson: A hash is only meaningful together with the function that produced it. Record the oracle with the number — and carry a secondary value like the input length, because two different oracles can otherwise be mistaken for a real difference.

critical_findings.summary: The full-map tooltip builds its unit line with I18n.t('zones.unit_' + zone.npcType). src/i18n/en.json defines unit_sentry, unit_fairy, unit_thug and so on, but there is no unit_normal — and the NPC type that maps to the 'Sentries' label is 'normal'.
critical_findings.impact: For the commonest NPC type the tooltip displays the raw key 'zones.unit_normal' instead of 'Sentries [100 HP • 1 Streak]'. Cosmetic, and it appears before and after the Phase 7 edit, so it is NOT a regression this refactor introduced.
critical_findings.how_it_was_caught: Incidentally, while comparing the tooltip's DOM before and after: the value read out of the live DOM was the literal string 'zones.unit_normal'. Confirmed by grepping src/i18n/en.json for unit_ keys. Note the t() helper returned the key rather than honouring the {defaultValue} the call passes, which is why it fails silently instead of falling back.
critical_findings.resolution: FIXED after the refactor, on explicit instruction. js/map.js now maps the type the way WorldRenderer already did: `zones.unit_${zone.npcType === "normal" ? "sentry" : zone.npcType}`. Verified live: the tooltip shows 'Sentries [100 HP • 1 Streak]' for a normal zone, 'Fairies [250 HP • 2 Streak]' for fairy, 'Thugs [750 HP • 5 Streak]' for thug. A new verifier, scratch/verify_i18n_unit_keys.mjs, guards the whole class rather than this instance: every one of the 22 npcTypes must resolve to a unit label either directly or through an explicit ALIASES table (currently just normal -> sentry), en and vi must define identical unit_* key sets, and js/map.js must still apply the alias. Its first run reported 'aliased: normal -> sentry', confirming unit_normal genuinely did not exist. Note the alias table is deliberately NOT 'whatever map.js computes' — mirroring map.js could never fail. WorldRenderer is the precedent that makes sentry the right target.
critical_findings.lesson: An i18n helper that returns the key on a miss turns a missing translation into plausible-looking output that survives review. A defaultValue argument is not a safety net unless the helper actually applies it.

critical_findings.summary: Two canvases are laid out larger than their bitmap: #minimap-canvas is width=180 rendered at 184 CSS px, and #full-map-canvas is width=880 rendered at 890. js/map.js divides screen offsets by canvas.width, so it already ignores the difference — meaning its zone hit-testing is off by ~2.2% horizontally (and exact vertically, where 460 == 460).
critical_findings.impact: Had I used the obvious canvas.width / rect.width correction in canvasPointFromEvent, it would have been 0.978 / 0.989 EVEN WITH NO TRANSFORM, silently shifting minimap and full-map hit-testing by ~2% as a side effect of a responsive-layout change. This was very close to shipping as an unnoticed behaviour change.
critical_findings.how_it_was_caught: By printing rect.width and offsetWidth next to canvas.width while verifying the helper, and noticing 184 vs 180. The first version of the helper did use canvas.width / rect.width, and the numbers are what exposed it.
critical_findings.resolution: First mitigated, then FIXED on explicit instruction. Mitigation: canvasPointFromEvent divides by the TRANSFORM scale — rect.width / canvas.offsetWidth, exactly 1 when unscaled — so the responsive work preserved the existing arithmetic bit-for-bit. Final fix: both canvases now render 1:1 with their bitmaps. The root cause was a 2px arithmetic error repeated through the layout chain — .minimap-widget is 196 with a 1px border and 6px padding, so its content box is 182, and the wrapper and canvas were BOTH declared 184. Corrected to wrapper 182 / height 127 and canvas 180x125 (the bitmap size); full map to wrapper 882x462 with align-self center to absorb the 8px spare in the card's 890 content box, and canvas 880x460. Verified live: minimap bitmap [180,125] == CSS [180,125] inside a [182,127] wrapper, full map [880,460] == [880,460] inside [882,462], neither clipped, and canvasPointFromEvent now returns the exact client offset. The 1,012-point scale sweep improved from 966 to 989 zone hits with 0 mismatches — the extra hits are the ~2% error disappearing — and the tooltip unit label resolves correctly for every type.
critical_findings.lesson: When adding a correction factor to existing coordinate maths, check what that factor equals at rest. If it is not 1, the 'fix' is also a behaviour change — and a ~2% one is small enough to pass review and large enough to move boundaries.

critical_findings.summary: verify_slice.mjs's 'no ref used by the body is missing from the import' check scanned the raw module text, so a domRefs name appearing only in PROSE counted as a use. Adding JSDoc that said 'the canvas is a fixed 1000x650 bitmap' made the check demand an import of `canvas` for src/core/GameLoop.js, which never touches that element.
critical_findings.impact: A false failure that would have been 'fixed' by importing an unused ref, or by wording the comment around the checker. Both are the wrong repair. It also masked the real signal: with comments counted as usage, a ref that had genuinely become unused would report as used.
critical_findings.how_it_was_caught: The failure detail named the identifier — 'canvas' — which does not appear anywhere in GameLoop.js's code, only in the comment I had just written. Naming the offending identifier in the message is what made this a two-minute diagnosis.
critical_findings.resolution: Comments are now blanked before the scan (stripComments). A name occurring only in a comment IS unused, so this makes the check stricter rather than looser.
critical_findings.lesson: Same trap as before, now confirmed a third time: any regex-based source check must blank comments and strings first, and any doc comment that names a symbol is a false input to it. Write the failure message to name the offending token, not just the assertion that failed.

critical_findings.summary: The guide's 'add a new sword' recipe lists 4 steps (data json, render js, ability js, register in SwordRegistry). It omits that src/systems/AbilitySystem.js dispatches the Z ability through an explicit if-chain and its own direct imports — the registry's `ability` field is not consulted.
critical_findings.impact: Follow the recipe as written and the new sword's Z key does nothing at all, with no error: activatePrimary falls through to Devourer's Gluttony, whose own guard rejects it because swordId !== 'devourer'. A silent no-op is the worst failure mode to debug from a recipe.
critical_findings.how_it_was_caught: By reading AbilitySystem.js to document the pattern accurately rather than transcribing the guide. The guide's own Phase 2 text does warn against wiring abilities via getSword(id).ability, but never states the consequence for the add-a-sword recipe.
critical_findings.resolution: Fixed in BOTH places. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §4 documents it as a mandatory step 5, with the exact two lines to add and why skipping it is silent; step 6 (the i18n strings) is spelled out too. The guide's section 6 has since been corrected as well, with an explicit '4 bước là chưa đủ — cần 6 bước' note, because that prose description is what someone reads before opening ARCHITECTURE.md.
critical_findings.lesson: A recipe is only as good as the last person who followed it. Documenting a pattern means finding the dispatch sites, not restating the plan — the plan and the code disagreed, and the code is what a new contributor will hit.

critical_findings.summary: SwordRegistry.js exports getSword(), getSwordData() and getSwordAbility(); none is called anywhere in the codebase. Only getSwordRenderer() is used (js/entities.js, js/game.js). Consequently the `ability` field of every registry entry is never read either.
critical_findings.impact: The registry looks like the ability dispatch point but is not, which is exactly what makes the guide's recipe incomplete (see guide-omits-ability-dispatch-step). Dead exports also invite a future contributor to start using the `ability` field, which would hand Overdrive a skill it has never had.
critical_findings.how_it_was_caught: Grepping for each exported helper while writing docs/ARCHITECTURE.md — the three names appeared only at their own definitions.
critical_findings.resolution: FIXED after the refactor, on explicit instruction. Removed getSword(), getSwordData() and getSwordAbility(), AND the `ability` field they exposed, along with the seven ability-module imports that existed only to populate it. The registry is now swordId -> { data, render }, which is what is actually consumed (getSwordRenderer only). This went further than the finding originally proposed: keeping the field while deleting its accessor would have left unreachable data that a future contributor could still pick up and use — and using it is the exact bug AbilitySystem.js's header warns about, so the object now carries a comment saying why there is no ability field. Before changing anything: confirmed verify_sword_strategy.mjs does not assert the field or the accessors, and confirmed the seven ability modules are imported by AbilitySystem.js anyway, so no import-time side effect became unreachable. Verified at runtime — render loop healthy (player moved 70px, so Player.draw -> getSwordRenderer(path) still runs) and Z on phase 17 set gluttonyCooldown to 9.73s with the HUD showing '[ Z — GLUTTONY ] 9.7s'. Build stayed at 90 modules, i.e. nothing was tree-shaken away.
critical_findings.lesson: An exported helper that nothing calls is a documented lie waiting to happen: it advertises an extension point that does not work. Either use it, or say plainly in the docs that it is not the dispatch path.

critical_findings.summary: README.md still said the legacy files were 'imported ... until Phase 2–6 refactoring is complete', listed line counts that were two refactors out of date (js/entities.js 5853 vs an actual 2735, js/game.js 4206 vs 1592), labelled js/i18n.js 'Active IIFE — Phase 6 target' when it has been dead since Phase 1, and its src/ tree omitted core/GameLoop.js, core/InputManager.js, systems/, render/, i18n/ and all of ui/ except toast.js.
critical_findings.impact: The README is the first thing a new contributor reads, and it pointed at the wrong files with wrong sizes — most dangerously at js/i18n.js as the i18n implementation.
critical_findings.how_it_was_caught: By reading it while writing docs/ARCHITECTURE.md and cross-checking the line counts, which came back roughly half the sizes claimed.
critical_findings.resolution: Directory tree completed, legacy table corrected with measured line counts and the dead-file warning, and a Responsive section plus a link to docs/ARCHITECTURE.md added.
critical_findings.lesson: Documentation rots silently and specifically: every number in that table was true when written. Prefer claims that cannot rot (what a file IS) over counts that can (how long it is), or state the date they were measured.

critical_findings.summary: I18n.t(key, params) fell back to the raw key when a lookup missed and never read params.defaultValue. 21 call sites already pass a defaultValue — every sword unlock toast, floating text and cutscene line — so they were all dead arguments. They happened to work only because those keys exist.
critical_findings.impact: This is the mechanism that turned missing-i18n-key-unit-normal from a visible error into invisible text: the tooltip rendered the string 'zones.unit_normal', which reads like a key rather than like a failure, so it survived review. Any future typo or half-added translation would fail the same silent way, in 21 places that look protected by a defaultValue.
critical_findings.how_it_was_caught: By reading t() to explain why the unit-label bug was silent, and noticing that the fallback chain was language -> English -> key, with params used only for {interpolation}.
critical_findings.resolution: t() now returns `typeof params.defaultValue === 'string' ? params.defaultValue : key`. Keys that resolve are unaffected, and a miss with no defaultValue still returns the key, so nothing that relies on the old behaviour changes. scratch/verify_i18n.mjs gained an explicit INTENTIONAL DIVERGENCE block asserting all four properties: the legacy copy ignored defaultValue, the new copy honours it, a miss with no defaultValue still yields the key, and defaultValue cannot override a key that resolves. The 761-key behavioural parity assertion still passes untouched.
critical_findings.lesson: A fallback argument that is silently ignored is worse than no fallback argument, because it advertises protection that does not exist — 21 call sites were written as though they were safe. When adding a guard, assert that it fires.

critical_findings.summary: Two quarantined dead artifacts were disposed of on explicit instruction: js/i18n.js (2,134 lines, dead since Phase 1 when src/main.js switched to src/i18n/I18n.js) and scratch/backup/dead-data-json/ (31 unreferenced sibling JSONs).
critical_findings.impact: js/i18n.js was the largest remaining trap in the repo: a 2,000-line file named exactly like the live i18n implementation, inviting an edit that would have had no effect. The dead JSON was a stale near-duplicate of the authoritative src/**/*.data.json files.
critical_findings.how_it_was_caught: Not a bug — a deliberate cleanup, gated on verification rather than assumption: confirmed no code imported or read either path, that data/ contained zero .json files, and that the only readers of js/i18n.js were the two parity scripts.
critical_findings.resolution: js/i18n.js moved to scratch/backup/obsolete/js-i18n.js, and scratch/verify_i18n.mjs + scratch/validate_phase1.mjs were re-pointed at the preserved copy so the check proving the extracted dictionaries were not altered still runs — retiring the file must not lose the evidence. dead-data-json/ deleted outright. scratch/diagnose_data_drift.mjs, whose sibling paths no longer exist, moved to obsolete/ with them. Suite stayed green at 19 scripts and the build at 90 modules.
critical_findings.lesson: Deleting dead code is only safe if you first prove nothing reads it, and only correct if you keep whatever still holds evidence. The i18n parity scripts were the reason to preserve a copy rather than delete outright; without them this would have destroyed the only reference the extraction could be checked against.

critical_findings.summary: Ten cutscene keys referenced by src/systems/cutscenes.data.js did not exist in src/i18n/{en,vi}.json — seven dialogue lines (flora_unlock_4, flora_p10_11, metallic_unlock_4, metallic_p10_10, hellfire_unlock_4, hellfire_p10_10, hellfire_p10_11) and three speaker names (speaker_grove, speaker_anvil, speaker_abyss). I18n.t() returns the key it was given when a lookup misses, so the player saw the literal text 'cutscene.flora_unlock_4' as dialogue and 'cutscene.speaker_grove' as the speaker name. Worse, the keys that DID exist for those six cutscenes held a DIFFERENT, older script, so lines 1..N showed text that did not match the code.
critical_findings.impact: A raw key on screen is the worst shape of a missing translation: 'cutscene.flora_unlock_4' reads like a label rather than an error, so it survives review, and it is what shipped. Six cutscenes were affected — the flora, metallic and hellfire unlock and phase-10 scenes, i.e. the three latest swords. The user reported it as 'flora dialogue name still not right', which was the same bug on the speaker keys.
critical_findings.how_it_was_caught: Reported by the user with a screenshot of the cutscene overlay. There was no automated check: the string is a perfectly valid translation as far as the dictionaries are concerned, and the code's `: "fallback"` branch never runs because I18n IS available — so nothing threw and nothing looked wrong to any existing verifier. Once a check existed, it found all ten on its first run.
critical_findings.resolution: Re-synced the dictionaries to the code, which the user confirmed is the authoritative script (evidence: for every cutscene EXCEPT these six, the dictionary text matches the code's fallback exactly, which proves the extraction was faithful and these six simply drifted; and soil_unlock_4 exists, so a 4-line unlock scene is normal). The 38 en and 37 vi values were written by scratch/resync_cutscene_dialogue.mjs, which extracts the code's string literals directly so en cannot be mistyped, inserts the 7 new keys beside their siblings rather than at the end of the object, and refuses to run unless re-stringifying both files reproduces them byte-for-byte. The 3 speaker names were added to both languages (ELDER GROVE / ANVIL OF WILL / INFERNAL ABYSS -> RỪNG CỔ THỤ / ĐE SẮT Ý CHÍ / VỰC THẲM HỎA NGỤC), following the existing convention that descriptive speaker names are translated while sword names stay English. THE VIETNAMESE IS A MACHINE FIRST PASS AND NEEDS A NATIVE SPEAKER'S REVIEW. verify_i18n.mjs and validate_phase1.mjs now exclude exactly these keys from their legacy deep-equality check, and assert that every other dictionary value still matches — a scoped, self-checking allowance rather than a blanket one.
critical_findings.lesson: Three of them. (1) A missing-key fallback that returns the key turns a broken translation into plausible-looking text; the fix is not just adding the key but making the class detectable. (2) Verify a claim about which artefact is stale before acting on it: the decisive evidence here was that every OTHER cutscene matched exactly — without that comparison, 'the code is newer' would have been an assumption, and acting on it would have destroyed a script. (3) My new checker initially reported btn_skip and hint as orphans because it only scanned src/; they are wired from index.html via data-i18n. A false positive in a fresh check is a bug in the check — widen the scan, do not silence the finding.

critical_findings.summary: Every phases.*.shortName in src/i18n/vi.json held the English text copied verbatim from en.json (all 77 of them, across devourer, overdrive, aquatic, soil, metallic, flora and hellfire), and the name portion of phases.*.name was left English too, so the string read 'Giai đoạn 10: Indestructible Soil Fortress'. A Vietnamese player saw 'GIAI ĐOẠN: SPROUT' in the HUD on every sword.
critical_findings.impact: Player-visible in Vietnamese mode on the HUD, the Library and the sword stand. It is worse than a missing key because it looks deliberate: the word 'GIAI ĐOẠN' was translated, so the line reads as finished Vietnamese at a glance while the one word that carries the meaning stays English. Reported by the user as a screenshot of 'GIAI ĐOẠN: SPROUT'.
critical_findings.how_it_was_caught: Reported by the user. No verifier could see it: en.json and vi.json were structurally identical with identical key sets, so every parity check passed, and the values were valid strings, so nothing fell back to a key. The dictionaries matched the legacy originals exactly too — the phase names had never been translated, rather than having regressed.
critical_findings.resolution: Wrote scratch/resync_phase_names.mjs: 77 translations as per-sword ordered arrays, applied so that each vi name agrees with the ability name already in skills.* rather than being invented twice (e.g. soil.10 'Indestructible Soil Fortress' -> 'Pháo Đài Thổ Nhưỡng Bất Diệt', matching achievements.soil_ascended.title). Two names whose English text could not be located inside the formatted 'Giai đoạn N: X' string are handled by an explicit per-key override ('soil.10', 'hellfire.10') instead of a looser regex. en.json was NOT touched. Scratch/verify_phase_names_translated.mjs now asserts that all 154 fields differ from en — a check that would have failed on all 154 before this fix. verify_i18n.mjs and validate_phase1.mjs were upgraded from a cutscene-only allowance to a leaf-path diff whose allowlist is exactly two documented scopes (cutscene resync, both languages; phase names, vi only), so any future drift outside them still fails. THE VIETNAMESE IS A MACHINE FIRST PASS AND NEEDS A NATIVE SPEAKER'S REVIEW.
critical_findings.lesson: Two of them. (1) Key-set parity is not translation: two dictionaries can have identical keys, identical shape and valid values while the Vietnamese one is English, so a translator you never diffs is a translator you do not have. The check that finds it must compare VALUES across languages, which is the opposite of what a parity verifier does. (2) The allowance in a parity script has to be as narrow as the change it excuses — replacing a cutscene-only regex with a cutscene-OR-phase-names predicate scoped per language is what keeps the new exception from becoming a blanket licence to edit the dictionaries. Verified end-to-end in the running game: the HUD now renders 'GIAI ĐOẠN: MẦM NON', 'PHẾ LIỆU', 'TÀN LỬA', 'ĐÓI KHÁT', 'GIỌT NƯỚC', 'LƯỠI ĐẤT' and 'THỦY NGÂN' with no English leaking.
